text: The British lawyer Cyril Radcliffe had never been to India. In the summer of nineteen forty-seven, he was given about five weeks to draw the line that would split it.
The Congress and the Muslim League, led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah, could not agree on one country. The League demanded a separate homeland for Muslims: Pakistan. Britain agreed to divide the land.
Sir, the census figures for the Punjab.
[wiping his glasses] And how long do I have?
About five weeks.
To divide... how many people?
Nearly four hundred million, sir.

At midnight on the fifteenth of August, nineteen forty-seven, India became free. In Delhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, the first Prime Minister, told the assembly that at the stroke of midnight, while the world slept, India would awake to life and freedom.
But Radcliffe's line was only announced two days later. Across Punjab and Bengal, millions of people woke up on the "wrong" side of a border they had never seen.

What followed was one of the largest migrations in human history. Somewhere between ten and twenty million people were forced from their homes. Trains arrived carrying only the dead. Estimates of those killed range from two hundred thousand to two million.
Gandhi spent Independence Day not in Delhi, but in Calcutta, fasting to stop the killing. Five months later, on the thirtieth of January, nineteen forty-eight, he was shot dead by a Hindu extremist.

India had another enormous problem. More than five hundred and sixty princely states, each ruled by its own maharaja or nawab, had to choose where to go. The man in charge was the Home Minister, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.
My family has ruled here for three hundred years.
And India would be honoured to keep you comfortable for three hundred more.
And in return?
[sliding the document across] One signature.
Most signed. Hyderabad held out until the Indian army moved in. Kashmir's ruler signed after raiders from Pakistan invaded, and the first war between India and Pakistan began.

Then India wrote its rules. A committee led by Dr Ambedkar drafted the Constitution, the longest written constitution of any country. It came into force on the twenty-sixth of January, nineteen fifty: Republic Day.

And remember Ashoka's wheel? When India chose its national flag, there were two wheels in the running. Gandhi's spinning wheel had been on the freedom flag for years. But in July nineteen forty-seven, the Constituent Assembly replaced it with the Ashoka Chakra. The emperor who apologised in stone, back at the centre of the flag, after two thousand years.

The new republic also did something many rich democracies took centuries to do: it gave every adult the vote, from day one. In the first election, about a hundred and seventy million people were eligible, and most of them could not read. So every party got a picture symbol.
The biggest election the world had ever seen, run on pictures.
India was free. It was also poor. And it was about to find out how close to broke a country can get.
